routes.description: Analytic idealism reduces reality to consciousness, the sole pre-theoretical given, while treating physicality as a perceptual representation of external mental states.
routes.successCriteria: Show that this ontology explains conscious experience, an objective structured world, and causal regularity more parsimoniously than an ontology containing nonmental matter.

motionBridge.description: Consciousness is the ontological foundation rather than an emergent product of matter.

centralBridges.description: Consciousness is the sole directly given category and additional nonmental categories require justification.
Physical properties are representations of mind-independent external mental states.
Intrinsic dispositions of external mental states can ground causal and physical regularity.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Strong emergence from nonconscious quantities lacks an intelligible explanatory bridge.
Dissociative boundaries distinguish individual minds from the wider field of mentality.

routes.description: Neutral monism avoids substance dualism and the hard problem without identifying the unknown underlying reality specifically as consciousness or mentality.
routes.successCriteria: Show that idealism adds no warranted explanation of objective structure, representation, boundaries, or causation beyond a neutral monist account.

motionBridge.description: Neutral monism is sufficient, so consciousness need not be declared reality's ontological foundation.

centralBridges.description: The underlying monistic reality should remain ontologically neutral where its nature is unknown.
An adequate ontology must explain the objective world's stable structure and regularities.
Consciousness talk can be reframed in terms of representations without positing a separate substance.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Idealism must explain the boundary between private and external states rather than merely name it.
Idealism must identify the source of causal organization within its proposed mental substrate.

sections.title: Foundational ontology and explanatory burden
sections.rationale: The opening clash establishes both sides' ontological routes and the principal burden concerning emergence, neutrality, and explanatory structure.

sections.title: External reality as representation
sections.rationale: This exchange tests whether idealism preserves a mind-independent world and whether calling its substrate mental explains anything further.

sections.title: Explanatory economy and the hard problem
sections.rationale: The moves compare idealism's removal of nonmental ontology with the objection that this maneuver may relocate rather than resolve explanation.

sections.title: Boundaries, causation, and physical regularity
sections.rationale: This section bears directly on whether dissociation and intrinsic dispositions can account for organisms, causation, and predictable physical structure.

sections.title: Representational models and experience
sections.rationale: The final selected exchange tests the neutral-monist representational proposal and idealism's claim that experienced models still presuppose mentality.

moves.speaker: Bernardo Kastrup
moves.proposition: Consciousness is the sole pre-theoretical datum, so reduction should begin from consciousness as a type of existence rather than add an inferred substrate.
moves.attributionBasis: The span is a continuous first-person answer by Bernardo Kastrup, with no competing speaker contribution inside the locked boundaries.

response.rationale: This is an opening constructive argument from epistemic immediacy and reductionist economy, so no earlier locked move is available or needed as a response target.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: The opening directly establishes the adopted foundational route, although its crucial epistemic-to-ontological bridge remains compressed.

precisionFindings.rationale: The distinction between individual consciousness and consciousness as a category is explicit, as is the proposal's reductionist framing.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The speaker presents idealism as the preferable account rather than certain truth, but direct givenness alone only partly warrants ontological priority.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The route from a directly given category to ontological reduction is intelligible, but the step from epistemic priority to ontological priority is material.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Pre-theoretical acquaintance and parsimony provide relevant support, while the exclusion of ontologically neutral alternatives is not established.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly advances the central bridge that consciousness is the starting category and rival categories incur an additional burden.

representationalCharity.rationale: No live alternative is represented or attacked in enough detail for charity to be tested.

moves.evidenceBasis: The locked span grounds the case in reductionism, the sole pre-theoretical datum, and an explicit distinction between personal minds and consciousness as a type.

moves.speaker: Bernardo Kastrup
moves.proposition: Strong emergence of qualitative experience from nonconscious physical quantities is explanatorily empty because no deduction connects physical parameters to experiential qualities.
moves.attributionBasis: The span remains within Bernardo Kastrup's uninterrupted answer and consistently uses his first-person evaluative framing of emergence.

response.rationale: No earlier con move exists in the locked chronology; the span constructively attacks emergentism in support of the pro route rather than answering a selected target.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: The move clearly identifies the explanatory gap, but turns that gap into categorical falsity without supplying the additional modal warrant.

precisionFindings.rationale: The claim is expressly limited to strong emergence from nonconscious physical quantities and distinguishes quantities from experiential qualities.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The absence of a supplied deduction supports an explanatory-gap objection, but not the categorical conclusion that strong emergence is false.

charity.alternative: Strong emergentism treats qualitative experience as a genuinely novel feature arising from organized nonconscious processes.
charity.decisiveQualification: An emergentist may posit primitive bridge laws or empirical dependence rather than claim present deductibility from physical parameters.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The move coherently identifies a missing deduction but makes an invalidly strong transition from absent explanation to metaphysical falsity.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The contrast between quantitative parameters and qualities is relevant, yet no evidence establishes that every possible emergent bridge is meaningless.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the subsidiary emergence bridge, but does not by itself complete the motion-level case for idealism.

representationalCharity.rationale: The argument treats strong emergence as an empty label and omits the alternative's possible appeal to primitive laws or empirical dependence.

moves.evidenceBasis: The locked span relies on the claimed absence of a deduction from physical parameters to experiential qualities and repeatedly expresses categorical confidence.

moves.speaker: Susan Blackmore
moves.proposition: Neutral monism accepts the hard problem's force and rejects dualism, but the unknown underlying unity need not be identified as mental.
moves.attributionBasis: The full span is Susan Blackmore's sustained response, marked by consistent first-person statements about her neutral-monist position and expertise limits.

response.rationale: The span principally constructs the con route by accepting the hard problem and monism while withholding a specifically mental characterization of the underlying unity.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: The constructive alternative is clearly differentiated from both dualism and full idealism, with its deliberate ontological restraint made explicit.

precisionFindings.rationale: Neutral monism, rejection of dualism, and uncertainty about the underlying unity are recoverable despite the span's conversational length.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The speaker advances ontological neutrality cautiously and repeatedly acknowledges uncertainty and limits in her knowledge of physics.

charity.alternative: Analytic idealism identifies the monistic basis as mental and uses dissociation to distinguish individual perspectives.
charity.decisiveQualification: Its external world is intended to be observer-independent and not composed of any individual's private mental contents.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Accepting monism while remaining neutral about the substrate is internally coherent and avoids the physical-to-mental emergence commitment.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The hard-problem discussion and acknowledged uncertainty support restraint, though neutrality is defended more as caution than through comparative evidence.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly establishes the con side's central claim that an unknown monistic basis need not be classified as mental.

representationalCharity.rationale: The idealist dissociation proposal is recognized, but its observer-independent external-world qualification is omitted and the position is left weaker.

moves.evidenceBasis: The span accepts the force of the hard problem, rejects consciousness as an extra product, states neutral monism, and declines the further idealist identification.

moves.speaker: Susan Blackmore
moves.proposition: Analytic idealism's dissociation analogy does not explain why the world divides and behaves with its observed physical structure.
moves.attributionBasis: Susan Blackmore continues without a speaker transition and directly develops her stated reason for declining the idealist account.

components.text: Consciousness is treated as the sole pre-theoretical datum.
Beginning from consciousness is claimed to yield the preferable reductive ontology.

response.rationale: The move does not dispute immediate consciousness; it diagnoses the proposed reduction as explanatorily inadequate because division and stable physical structure remain unaccounted for.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: The structural defect and its consequence for idealism's claimed adequacy are explicit, though the comparison with physical explanation remains compressed.

precisionFindings.rationale: The missing explanatory target is clear, but the precise standard by which physical structure would count as explained remains implicit.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The speaker cautiously reports that idealism has not supplied the needed structure, while only briefly supporting the favorable comparison with physical theory.

charity.alternative: Analytic idealism uses dissociation to explain differentiated perspectives within a single mental reality.
charity.decisiveQualification: Physical regularities are intended to remain valid as representations of the underlying mental dynamics.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The demand for an account of differentiation and regularity follows coherently from judging an ontology by explanatory adequacy.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Observed physical structure is a relevant comparison point, but the span supplies few specifics and does not show that idealism cannot reproduce it.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The objection directly advances the central con requirement that an ontology explain stable objective structure and behavior.

representationalCharity.rationale: The dissociation analogy is identified accurately, but the idealist treatment of physical laws as representations is not included.

moves.evidenceBasis: The locked span challenges the dissociation analogy through the unexplained division of the world and contrasts this with the apparent structural resources of physics.

moves.speaker: Bernardo Kastrup
moves.proposition: Analytic idealism preserves an external, observer-independent world by treating physical perception as representation of external mental states, not as creation by personal minds.
moves.attributionBasis: The span is Bernardo Kastrup's uninterrupted clarification, repeatedly distinguishing his private mental states from an external mental world.

components.text: The hard problem motivates rejection of physical-to-mental emergence and dualism.
The unknown monistic basis need not be identified specifically as mental.
Idealism must explain differentiation between individual and external states.
Idealism must explain the world's stable physical structure and behavior.

response.rationale: The move explains observer independence and perceptual representation while arguing that mentality avoids a new category, but it does not yet explain the source of stable physical regularities.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It directly resolves the solipsism and differentiation misunderstanding and contacts the neutrality issue, while leaving the structural challenge unanswered.

precisionFindings.rationale: The span repeatedly distinguishes personal contents, external mental states, perceptual representations, and observer independence in stable terms.

calibrationFindings.rationale: As an internal exposition of analytic idealism the claims are qualified by that framework, though the analogy does not establish that the external substrate is mental.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The representational architecture is internally consistent, but the analogy with inaccessible private thoughts does not establish ontological sameness.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The thought-access analogy and category economy support intelligibility, while the decisive classification of the external substrate remains asserted.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly advances the pro central bridge that physical properties represent observer-independent external mental states.

representationalCharity.rationale: The response clarifies a misunderstanding but does not fully reconstruct the strongest neutral-monist alternative and its qualification.

moves.evidenceBasis: The span distinguishes private and external mentality, explains perception as an intermediary dashboard-like representation, and denies dependence on personal observers.

moves.speaker: Susan Blackmore
moves.proposition: Calling an inaccessible external substrate mental adds no clear explanation of the representations or the machinery that constructs them.
moves.attributionBasis: Susan Blackmore begins immediately after the clarification and sustains the same critical question about labeling and representational machinery throughout the span.

components.text: The external world is independent of individual observers and their private contents.
Perception is an internal representation of an inaccessible external substrate.
The represented external substrate is specifically mental rather than ontologically neutral.

response.rationale: The move accepts the inaccessible substrate and representational setup for argument's sake, then identifies the mental label's missing mechanism and denies that it adds explanatory value.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Every indispensable component is contacted and the alleged defect's consequence is explicit, although the critique does not establish that no mental account could supply machinery.

precisionFindings.rationale: The objection consistently separates the substrate's label from the machinery responsible for representations and is framed with explicit uncertainty.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The span asks what the mental classification explains and presents its negative assessment cautiously rather than claiming a categorical refutation.

charity.alternative: Analytic idealism treats physical appearances as representations of an observer-independent external mental reality.
charity.decisiveQualification: Its claimed gain is ontological economy and avoidance of a new nonmental category, not merely a verbal relabeling.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The distinction between renaming a substrate and explaining the construction of representations is clear and directly supports the diagnostic conclusion.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The critique is grounded in explanatory burden and identifies a specific missing mechanism, with only a bounded gap about possible idealist answers.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the pro representation bridge by questioning both the mental classification and its alleged explanatory contribution.

representationalCharity.rationale: The representational architecture is acknowledged, but the ontological-economy rationale is reduced too nearly to a mere change of label.

moves.evidenceBasis: The locked span accepts the inaccessible represented substrate, isolates the mental classification, and asks for the machinery producing predictive representations.

moves.speaker: Bernardo Kastrup
moves.proposition: Idealism gains explanatory economy by removing the unnecessary nonmental category whose alleged production of mentality creates the hard problem.
moves.attributionBasis: The span is a continuous Bernardo Kastrup reply using his established vocabulary of ontological categories, dissociation, perception, and mental causation.

components.text: Calling the external substrate mental appears to add no explanatory value.
The source and machinery of perceptual representations remain unexplained.

response.rationale: The answer reframes the gain as removal of a problematic category and supplies a mental-to-mental causal sketch involving dissociation, sensory impingement, and evolutionary amplification.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Both components receive direct answers, but the account of dissociation and its evolutionary emergence is highly compressed and partly stipulative.

precisionFindings.rationale: The economy argument is recoverable, but dissociation, possibility, inevitability, and explanatory success are moved between without stable scope conditions.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The span calls the rival setup impossible and treats possible dissociation as eventually inevitable without supplying warrants adequate to those necessities.

charity.alternative: Neutral monism retains an unknown substrate without committing to physical-to-mental production.
charity.decisiveQualification: It can reject both nonmental substance and a separate emergence relation while declining to classify the substrate as mental.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Ontological economy is intelligible, but the moves from possibility to inevitability and from everyday mental interaction to world perception are materially underbridged.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Everyday mental influence and sensory evolution are relevant analogies, while dissociation and its origin carry substantial weight as unsupported assertions.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly supports the central pro economy claim that no additional nonmental category is required to account for perception.

representationalCharity.rationale: The answer recasts the neutral challenge as a nonmental-emergence theory, omitting the opponent's decisive refusal of that commitment.

moves.evidenceBasis: The span argues from category removal, proposes dissociative separation, and sketches perception through causal impingement and evolved sensory amplification.

moves.speaker: Susan Blackmore
moves.proposition: The sharp boundary between accessible internal states and inaccessible external mental states requires explanation rather than assumption.
moves.attributionBasis: Susan Blackmore takes the next uninterrupted turn and focuses consistently on the boundary presupposed by Bernardo Kastrup's immediately preceding account.

components.text: Removing a nonmental category is claimed to dissolve the hard problem.
Dissociated internal states receive information through a boundary from external states.

response.rationale: The reply isolates the asserted internal-external boundary and asks what produces it and how it relates to bodily properties, without addressing the broader economy claim.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: The boundary mechanism is contacted precisely, but it is only one component of the stronger economy-and-perception answer being challenged.

precisionFindings.rationale: The interrogative demand has a clear referent: the boundary separating accessible internal states from inaccessible external mental states.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move asks for an explanation of an acknowledged boundary and does not claim more than the preceding account makes available.

charity.alternative: Analytic idealism locates personal minds within dissociative boundaries manifested through organisms.
charity.decisiveQualification: The body is proposed as the perceptual appearance of the boundary, not as a material producer of consciousness.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Given the asserted separation, asking what constitutes and sustains the boundary follows directly and introduces no additional inferential burden.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The question is tightly grounded in the preceding distinction and identifies a necessary explanatory step rather than relying on speculative evidence.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly advances the subsidiary con boundary bridge but does not independently establish the motion-level sufficiency of neutral monism.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply accurately tracks dissociation and bodily manifestation while pressing for an explanation rather than replacing the view with a caricature.

moves.evidenceBasis: The locked span identifies the sharp internal-external division and asks both what makes it and whether bodily properties are doing the explanatory work.

moves.speaker: Bernardo Kastrup
moves.proposition: Bodily surfaces represent dissociative boundaries, while external mentality's intrinsic dispositions yield repeatable causal effects and preserve physical and chemical regularities.
moves.attributionBasis: Bernardo Kastrup answers continuously across the span, first addressing bodily boundaries and then extending the account to dispositions and physical regularity.

components.text: Idealism must explain why differentiated subjects or regions arise.
Idealism must account for stable physical structure and repeatable behavior.
A sharp division between internal and external mental states is presupposed.
The source and bodily manifestation of that boundary require explanation.

response.rationale: The span identifies bodily surfaces as appearances of dissociative boundaries, sketches their selection history, and attributes regularity to intrinsic dispositions of external mentality.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: All indispensable demands are expressly contacted, but several answers rest on stipulation, circular disposition language, or an unsupported possibility-to-occurrence transition.

precisionFindings.rationale: The boundary and regularity claims are recoverable, but dissociation, inherent disposition, archetype, and mechanistic behavior shift explanatory roles across a broad scope.

calibrationFindings.rationale: First-person hedges occur, but possibility is treated as sufficient for occurrence and dispositions are presented as explaining predictable universal regularity.

charity.alternative: The con demand seeks a causal account of boundaries and regularity rather than an ultimate purpose for nature.
charity.decisiveQualification: Identifying the body as a boundary's appearance does not by itself explain the boundary's occurrence or stable structural effects.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The route is intelligible, but possibility-to-actuality reasoning and the appeal to dispositions as explanations of regularity leave material inferential gaps.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Biological surfaces and natural selection supply suggestive analogies, while dissociation, universal dispositions, and repeated causation are mostly asserted.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly supports the central pro causality bridge and also materially addresses the subsidiary dissociation requirement.

representationalCharity.rationale: The answer partly recasts a request for causal mechanism as an unproductive request for ultimate purpose, weakening the live objection.

moves.evidenceBasis: The locked span links bodily surfaces to dissociation, invokes reproduction and selection, and grounds physical predictability in intrinsic mental dispositions.

moves.speaker: Susan Blackmore
moves.proposition: A neutral-monist representational account avoids the hard problem by locating experience in a bat's models rather than in a separately assumed physical bat.
moves.attributionBasis: The entire span is Susan Blackmore's uninterrupted presentation of her neutral-monist and representational alternative, including its explicit limitations.

components.text: Only removal of a nonmental category is claimed to avoid the hard problem.
Mental-to-mental causation is offered as the machinery of representation.

response.rationale: The move offers a neutral representational route that avoids initially positing a physical bat, thereby challenging idealism's claimed exclusivity without answering its causal machinery.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: The decisive hard-problem and economy claim is contacted through a genuine alternative, but the earlier account of representational causation is left untouched.

precisionFindings.rationale: The distinction between a bat, its representations, and what those representations specify is stable, and the proposal's exploratory status is explicit.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The speaker explicitly says the route avoids rather than solves the hard problem and presents it as a proposal for further development.

charity.alternative: Analytic idealism also offers a monistic representational account and treats physical appearances as mental models.
charity.decisiveQualification: Idealism identifies mentality as the starting category because conscious experience is directly known, whereas the neutral substrate is not.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Relocating the bat question to representations is intelligible, but the claim that a representation determines what experience is like remains underexplained.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Representational modeling provides a relevant conceptual route, yet the span does not explain why models have experiential character at all.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly advances the central con bridge that consciousness discourse can be reframed representationally without a separate substance.

representationalCharity.rationale: The idealist project is recognized as a serious monist alternative, with only its epistemic reason for specifying mentality left compressed.

moves.evidenceBasis: The span identifies neutral monism, rejects a separately assumed physical subject, and relocates the what-it-is-like question to representational models.

moves.speaker: Bernardo Kastrup
moves.proposition: Representational self-models can be delusions, but their experienced existence still requires mentality and therefore does not rescue materialist illusionism.
moves.attributionBasis: Bernardo Kastrup speaks throughout the long span, consistently distinguishing Susan Blackmore's neutral view from materialist forms of illusionism.

components.text: Neutral monism is distinguished from materialist or dualist emergence theories.
Experience is located in a subject's representational model rather than a separately assumed physical subject.
The representational move is claimed to avoid the hard problem.

response.rationale: The response accepts the neutral-monist version's avoidance claim and model account, then argues that materialist illusionism fails because any experienced model still presupposes mentality.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: All target components are explicitly engaged and the decisive qualification is honored, though most critical force applies to materialism rather than neutral monism.

precisionFindings.rationale: Models, delusions, experience, and materialist illusionism remain distinguishable, and the neutral-monist exception is repeatedly made explicit.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The necessity of an experiencer for an experienced illusion is well motivated, but its extension to idealism as the required ontology remains compressed.

charity.alternative: Neutral monism treats experience as associated with representational models without deriving it from an independently assumed physical substance.
charity.decisiveQualification: Because the view is not materialist, the neuroactivity regress directed at materialist illusionism does not defeat it.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The regress objection to materialist modeling and the point that experienced illusions remain experiences are coherent, despite limited force against neutrality.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The conceptual regress and experiential premise provide substantial support, while the further ontological conclusion is not independently demonstrated.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly tests the central con models bridge, but concedes that its neutral-monist form avoids the specific hard problem under discussion.

representationalCharity.rationale: The response clearly distinguishes the opponent's neutral monism from materialist illusionism and expressly limits its main criticism accordingly.

moves.evidenceBasis: The span accepts representational self-models and self-delusion, separates neutral monism from materialism, and develops a regress against neuroactivity-only models.

moves.speaker: Susan Blackmore
moves.proposition: If experience attaches to models, consistency suggests that fleeting models throughout predictive hierarchies have something it is like to be them, not only the self-model.
moves.attributionBasis: Susan Blackmore speaks continuously across the locked span and develops one consistent question about experience across levels of representational processing.

components.text: Experienced representational models still instantiate mentality.
The apparently persisting personal self can be a constructed model or delusion.
Materialist illusionism fails because modeling only postpones the experiential problem.

response.rationale: The reply accepts the model premise and extends its scope to fleeting representations throughout a predictive hierarchy, but does not answer the argument against materialist illusionism.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It develops a substantive implication of the model premise and contacts the self-model discussion, while leaving the target's principal materialist critique unanswered.

precisionFindings.rationale: The claim consistently ranges over representational models at multiple predictive levels and explicitly marks the proposal as the speaker's considered view.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Consistency supplies a reason to distribute experience across models, but the individuation and experiential status of every fleeting model remain unsupported.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The consistency argument is intelligible, but it assumes without adequate bridge that each computational representation is a distinct experiential subject.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Predictive-hierarchy examples clarify the proposal, while the crucial premise that every transient model has experience is asserted rather than evidenced.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move materially advances the central con representational route, though it does not independently show the sufficiency of ontological neutrality.

representationalCharity.rationale: The earlier model premise is extended rather than reconstructing and testing the strongest opposing alternative with its decisive qualification.

moves.evidenceBasis: The locked span contrasts the ephemeral self-model with numerous lower-level predictive models and argues that consistency assigns experience throughout the hierarchy.
